notes.title: Introduction to data structures – revision sheet
notes.md:
## Definition and classification
- Data structure = organised way of storing data for efficient access and change; ADT = data + operations, implementation hidden
- **Primitive**: int, char, float, double, pointer (machine-level)
- **Non-primitive** → **linear** (array, stack, queue, linked list) | **non-linear** (tree, graph)
- Static (array, fixed size) vs dynamic (linked list); homogeneous (array) vs heterogeneous (structure)
- Choosing: hierarchy → tree; network → graph; undo/recursion → stack; printer jobs/BFS → queue
- Data → information; field → record → file

## Operations
Traversing, searching, inserting, deleting, sorting, merging

## Complexity
- Time / space as a function of input size n; best, average, worst case; time–space trade-off
- O (upper), Ω (lower), Θ (tight), o (strictly smaller); constants and lower terms dropped
- Growth: 1 < log n < √n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2ⁿ < n!
| Code pattern | Time |
|---|---|
| single loop to n | O(n) |
| i = i × 2 (or × 3) | O(log n) |
| i × i ≤ n | O(√n) |
| two nested loops to n | O(n²) |
| j from i to n (n = 4 → 10 steps) | O(n²) |
| three nested loops | O(n³) |
| naive Fibonacci | O(2ⁿ) |
- Recurrences: T(n−1) + 1 → n; T(n/2) + 1 → log n; 2T(n/2) + 1 → n; 2T(n/2) + n → n log n
- Algorithm properties (Knuth): finiteness, definiteness, input, output, effectiveness

notes.title: Primitive data structures – revision sheet
notes.md:
## Integers
- 2's complement: n bits → −2ⁿ⁻¹ … 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1 (8-bit −128…127; 32-bit ±2.1 × 10⁹); −5 = 11111011
- Unsigned 16-bit 0…65,535; unsigned arithmetic wraps (255 + 1 = 0 in 8 bits; 250 + 10 = 4)
- Operations: + − × / % (17 / 5 = 3, 17 % 5 = 2), comparison, bitwise
- Little-endian stores the least significant byte first (0x12345678 → 78 56 34 12)

## Characters
- ASCII 7-bit ('A' 65 = 01000001, 'a' 97, '0' 48, space 32); Unicode/UTF-8 for Kannada etc.
- Arithmetic on codes: 'a' + 2 = 'c'; c − '0' gives a digit's value; lowercase − 32 = uppercase

## Floating point
- IEEE 754: float 1 + 8 + 23 (≈ 7 digits), double 1 + 11 + 52 (≈ 15–16 digits); normalized mantissa starts with 1
- 0.1 is not exact (0.5 is) – never compare floats with ==; store money as integer paise

## Strings
- C: char array ending in '\0' ("KEA" = 4 bytes; sizeof("") = 1); Pascal: length byte
- Representations: fixed-length, variable-length (terminator or length), linked
- Pointer idioms: length `while (*p) p++; return p − s;`; copy `while ((*d++ = *s++));`; reverse with two pointers (⌊n/2⌋ swaps); atoi `n = n*10 + (*p − '0')`
- Library: strlen, strcpy, strncpy, strcat (O(len1 + len2)), strcmp (code order: 'Z' < 'a'), strchr, strstr, strtok
- Array of char pointers saves space for ragged strings; sort by swapping pointers; compare with strcmp, not ==

notes.title: Arrays – revision sheet
notes.md:
## Storage representation
- 1-D: Loc(A[i]) = Base + w × (i − LB); number of elements = UB − LB + 1
- 2-D (m × n): row-major Loc = Base + w × (n × (i − LB₁) + (j − LB₂)); column-major Base + w × (m × (j − LB₂) + (i − LB₁))
  - char a[100][100] at 0 → a[40][50] = 4050; A[5][4], w = 4, base 100 → A[3][2] = 156 (row) / 152 (column)
- 3-D: A[1][2][3] of A[2][3][4] = 1·12 + 2·4 + 3 = 23 elements from the base
- Special matrices: lower triangular n(n + 1)/2 (index i(i+1)/2 + j), tridiagonal 3n − 2, diagonal n; sparse → triplets (header + one row per non-zero)

## Insertion and deletion (n elements)
- Insert at pos: check overflow; shift a[n−1]…a[pos] right (from the end); place; n++ → O(n) (front worst, end O(1))
- Delete at pos: shift a[pos+1]…a[n−1] left; n−− → n − pos − 1 moves; unordered delete: copy last element in, O(1)
- Insert into a sorted array: find the position, then shift

## Advantages / disadvantages
| Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|
| O(1) random access | fixed size (overflow or waste) |
| no pointer overhead | O(n) insert/delete in the middle |
| simple, cache-friendly | needs one contiguous block |
- Dynamic arrays grow by doubling (amortised O(1) append); parallel arrays

notes.title: Linked lists – revision sheet
notes.md:
## Basics
- Node = data + pointer(s): `struct node { int data; struct node *next; };` (self-referential)
- Create: `t = (struct node *) malloc(sizeof(struct node));` (NULL → overflow); release: `free(t)`; AVAIL list (Lipschutz)
- Empty: head == NULL; deleting from empty = underflow; forgetting free = memory leak; using freed node = dangling pointer

## Operations (singly, head pointer only)
| Operation | Code | Time |
|---|---|---|
| insert at front | t->next = head; head = t | O(1) |
| insert after p | t->next = p->next; p->next = t | O(1) |
| insert at end | traverse (O(1) with tail) | O(n) |
| delete first | tmp = head; head = head->next; free(tmp) | O(1) |
| delete last | find second-last | O(n) |
| search / k-th element | traverse | O(n) |
- Reverse iteratively O(n); middle by slow/fast pointers; cycle by Floyd's method; merge sorted lists O(m + n)

## Variants
- Circular: last → first, no NULL; traverse with do … while (p != head); round-robin, Josephus; front insert O(1) with a last pointer
- Doubly (two-way): prev + data + next (3 fields, 2n pointers); delete p: p->prev->next = p->next; p->next->prev = p->prev
- Header lists: grounded (last → NULL) or circular (last → header)
- Uses: polynomials (coefficient, exponent nodes), stacks and queues, hash chaining, sparse matrices
- Prefer lists for frequent insert/delete and unknown size; arrays for random access
